readerTitle: The meeting that hears trouble before it quits
caseNote: 가상 사례 (물류 창고, 소프트웨어 팀) · 개념 출처는 Andy Grove의 High Output Management
insight: 원온원은 관리자가 진행 상황을 확인하는 자리가 아니라, 직원이 아직 말하지 않은 작은 문제를 일찍 꺼내게 만드는 정기적인 통로다.
misconception: 원온원은 문제가 생겼을 때 하는 면담이거나, 업무 진행 상황을 점검하는 회의다. 정기 회의만 잡아 두면 원온원을 잘하고 있는 것이다.

sources.text: Grove, A. S. (1983). High Output Management. Random House. (원온원은 직원의 회의이며 의제를 직원이 정한다는 원칙)
창고와 소프트웨어 팀 사례는 설명용 가상 사례

factChecks.note: Grove가 High Output Management에서 원온원을 '부하 직원의 회의'로 보고, 의제를 직원이 정해야 한다고 쓴 내용을 원문으로 다시 확인하세요. 카드에는 구체적인 시간 수치를 인용하지 않고 원칙만 적었습니다.
모든 인물, 회사, 사직 사례는 가상입니다. 연구 통계는 넣지 않았습니다.

cards.title: Two resignations. Same week. Same surprise.
body: Dana runs a loading crew at a parcel warehouse. Sam writes code at a software startup. Both are reliable, and both quit on the same Friday.
Their managers say the same thing: *I had no idea.* One manager barely met with his people. The other met with his every week. Neither heard it coming.

image.label: A warehouse and an office, each with an empty chair
image.brief: 화면을 반으로 나눈 3D 클레이 스타일 일러스트. 왼쪽은 물류 창고 하역장, 오른쪽은 소프트웨어 사무실. 양쪽 모두 빈 의자 위에 사직서 봉투가 놓여 있음. 실제 회사 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: You have 30 minutes a week per lead.
body: You supervise six team leads at a warehouse that runs two shifts. The floor is loud, busy and short-staffed.
You can give each lead about 30 minutes a week. How do you use it?

options.text: Walk the floor daily and ask each lead, "Everything okay?"
options.feedback: You stay visible and catch urgent problems. But a quick question in front of the crew rarely gets an honest answer about schedules, pay or a tough coworker.

options.text: A short, private, regular chat with each lead, where they bring the topics
options.feedback: It costs a fixed slot every week. In return, leads get a predictable place to raise small problems before they grow.

options.text: Keep an open door and save bigger talks for the yearly review
options.feedback: It saves time now. But most people won't walk in to raise a small worry, so you hear about it when it's already a resignation.

cards.title: No meeting in one. The wrong meeting in the other.
body: At the warehouse, Dana's new shift clashed with her child's school hours. She mentioned it once, in passing, during a rush. Nobody followed up. A rival warehouse offered day shifts.

At the startup, Sam had a weekly meeting with his manager. Every one was a ticket-by-ticket status check. Sam wanted bigger projects but never found a moment to say so. Another company offered him one.
Two different businesses. The same missing conversation.

image.label: Two timelines with a missed signal on each
image.brief: 두 개의 가로 타임라인. 위쪽은 창고(Dana), 아래쪽은 소프트웨어 팀(Sam). 각 타임라인 초반에 작은 말풍선 신호("School hours...", "Bigger projects?")가 있고, 끝에는 사직서 아이콘. 신호와 사직 사이 구간을 회색으로 강조.

cards.title: One-on-ones
body: A **one-on-one** is a regular, private meeting between a manager and one person on their team. It is mainly *their* meeting, not yours.
Andy Grove, who ran Intel, made this point in his 1983 book *High Output Management*: the employee should set the agenda.
Status updates can travel by message or board. A one-on-one exists for what doesn't travel well: worries, ideas, career goals and friction with coworkers.

cards.title: Small habits make it work.
body: The format matters less than a few steady habits:
list: **Keep the rhythm:** same slot, rarely cancelled
**Their topics first:** your items go last
**Ask open questions:** "What's getting in your way?"
**Write it down:** a short note of what you agreed
**Follow up:** start next time with what you promised
cards.callout: Follow-up is what turns a chat into trust.
cards.softwareNote: On a remote software team, a one-on-one may be the only time a person talks with their manager outside group calls. Keep the camera on, and keep the shared notes in one running document.

cards.title: It doesn't need a meeting room.
body: On a warehouse floor, a one-on-one might be 15 minutes in the break room before shift, or a walk around the yard. It still needs privacy and a fixed time.
At the startup, it might be 30 minutes on a video call every week. A newer hire may need weekly time. A seasoned lead may prefer every two weeks.
The constant is the purpose: a reliable place for the other person to speak.

cards.title: One-on-ones have real costs.
body: Six leads at 30 minutes each is three hours a week. If you can't protect that time, fewer reliable meetings beat many cancelled ones. Cancelling often tells people they rank last.
They also don't replace feedback in the moment. Waiting a week to mention a safety slip is too long.
And a meeting on the calendar is not proof it works. Sam's manager met weekly and still missed everything.

cards.title: Your one-on-ones became status meetings.
body: You manage four engineers at a software company. Your weekly one-on-ones now mostly repeat what the team said at the daily stand-up meeting. Engineers seem bored.
What do you change?

options.text: Cancel them. Stand-up already covers everything
options.feedback: You get time back, but you remove the only private channel. Career and team issues rarely come up in a group update.

options.text: Move status to written updates and ask each engineer to bring the first topic
options.feedback: It takes a few awkward weeks while people learn to fill the time. Then the meeting starts carrying what stand-up can't.

options.text: Keep them, but review every ticket in more detail
options.feedback: You'll know the work better. But the meeting becomes more of your agenda, and less room is left for theirs.

cards.title: Give your people a regular place to tell you things.
body: A one-on-one is the employee's meeting. Its job is to surface small problems while they're still small.
**Try it today:** at your next one-on-one, open with "What's on your mind this week?" and say nothing until they answer.
